main_damage_causes: Agency transfer to Scabior: Greyback's dominant role in the Snatchers capture and Malfoy Manor sequences — his most substantial appearances in the later books — is systematically reassigned to the invented character Scabior, hollowing out his function as a commanding, independently menacing figure.

Loss of defining psychology at the Astronomy Tower: The film omits the crucial revelation that Greyback attacks outside the full moon by choice, stripping away the trait that makes him uniquely horrifying even among werewolves and removing Dumbledore's direct engagement with this horror.

Reduction from autonomous predator to subordinate weapon: Across HBP film appearances, Greyback is repositioned as an instrument deployed on Bellatrix's signal rather than as a self-directed, calculating monster with his own agenda — fundamentally misrepresenting the power dynamic the books establish between him and the Death Eater inner circle.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film HBP Scene 3 (Borgin & Burkes back courtyard) – Greyback present at Dark Mark ceremony
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book establishes Greyback as a hired savage who operates outside the inner Death Eater circle; he is not branded with the Dark Mark and is used instrumentally by Voldemort. His relationship to Draco/Malfoy is purely as a threatening tool Draco invokes to intimidate Borgin. There is no scene of Greyback participating in any Dark Mark or initiation ritual.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film places Greyback in the back courtyard of Borgin & Burkes alongside Bellatrix, Narcissa, and Draco during what appears to be a Dark Mark ceremony/ritual around a cauldron, positioning him as an intimate insider of Death Eater inner-circle activity.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book is explicit that Greyback is not granted the Dark Mark and is kept at arm's length from the inner circle — this outsider status is a defining character trait. Placing him at what looks like an initiation ritual alongside the Malfoys and Bellatrix misrepresents his structural position in Voldemort's hierarchy and undermines a narratively important detail paid off in DH when Greyback cannot summon Voldemort directly.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film HBP Scene 4 (Burrow attack) – Greyback attacks the Burrow on Bellatrix's signal
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The Burrow attack does not occur in the book at all. More relevantly, the book characterizes Greyback as a werewolf who positions himself near victims at the full moon and bites strategically; his violence is predatory and self-directed, not subordinately triggered by Bellatrix's clicking signal.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Greyback lurks in the reeds and advances on command when Bellatrix makes a clicking noise like a signal, behaving as her obedient attack animal rather than as an independent, calculating predator. He is used as a weapon she deploys.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book stresses that Greyback acts on his own predatory agenda — he positions himself near victims by his own planning, and even Voldemort merely offers him prey as incentive rather than commanding him. Reducing him to Bellatrix's trained beast on a leash strips away his autonomous menace and his defining characteristic of independent, calculating savagery.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film HBP Scene 5/6 (Astronomy Tower) – Greyback's dialogue reduced to one line about finishing Draco
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Greyback has extensive, viscerally threatening dialogue at the tower: he boasts about attacking outside the full moon, savors the prospect of ripping throats, taunts Dumbledore about eating children, picks his teeth with a yellow fingernail, and makes an independent move to kill Dumbledore himself ('I'll do it,' snarling forward). His physical presence — the smell of blood, dirt, and sweat, the pointed teeth, the blood trickling down his chin — is elaborately established. Dumbledore engages him directly, noting with disgust that he attacks outside the full moon.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Greyback's tower presence is reduced to a single line: 'He doesn't have the stomach. Like his father. Let me finish him. In my own way.' He has no further dialogue, no physical grotesque description is conveyed through action, no independent lunge toward Dumbledore, and the Dumbledore-Greyback exchange about attacking outside the full moon is entirely absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The tower scene is the primary moment where Greyback's most disturbing trait — that he attacks outside the full moon by choice, having developed a taste for human flesh — is established in the books. Dumbledore's horrified recognition of this is important characterization for both figures. The film loses all of this, reducing Greyback from a multidimensional monster with distinct, chilling psychology to a generic brute with one disposable line.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film DH1 Scene 10 (Forest capture) – Scabior takes Greyback's dominant role in interrogation
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Greyback is unambiguously the leader of the Snatchers and dominates the entire capture interrogation sequence. He delivers most of the threatening lines, physically strikes Harry, presses his finger to Harry's scar, sniffs out Harry's identity, makes the decision to go to Malfoy Manor rather than the Ministry, and asserts authority over the group ('Who's in charge here?'). The relish with which he eyes Hermione ('what a treat... I do enjoy the softness of the skin') establishes him as sexually predatory, adding another dimension to his menace.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Scabior takes the dominant speaking role throughout the capture scene. He delivers the 'your boyfriend will get worse than that' line (which in the book is Greyback's), does the atmospheric sniffing of Hermione's neck, and leads most of the questioning. Greyback is physically present (his boot on Ron's neck) but largely silent, with his lines reassigned to Scabior. The decision about where to take the prisoners also shifts to Scabior ('Change of plans, boys. We won't be taking this lot to the Ministry').
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is the most significant single scene in which Greyback's agency is directly transferred to another character. The book's capture sequence is one of Greyback's most important appearances — it establishes his cunning, his predatory fixation on Hermione, his command authority, and the detail that he lacks the Dark Mark (can't summon Voldemort). All of these characterization beats are either lost or given to Scabior, a minor character invented for the films. This damages audience understanding of who Greyback is and why he is dangerous.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film DH1 Scene 11-12 (Malfoy Manor arrival and interior) – Greyback's confrontation with Bellatrix over the sword reassigned to Scabior
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, it is Greyback who confronts Bellatrix when she tries to take the Sword of Gryffindor from his group — he snarls 'How dare you? Release me, woman!' and bares his teeth, and it is Greyback whom Bellatrix forces to his knees. He then takes the prisoners to the cellar and makes his leering threat to Ron about getting 'a bit of the girl.' This sequence reveals both his defiance of authority and his predatory sexuality as independent character traits.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The confrontation over the sword is reassigned to Scabior, who shouts 'How dare you! Release me, woman!' It is Scabior who is stunned and forced to his knees. Greyback is simply present and then exits with Scabior. The cellar-escort threat to Ron about Hermione is entirely absent. Wormtail, not Greyback, takes the prisoners to the cellar.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Again Greyback's agency and distinctive voice are transferred to Scabior. The book's version reveals important nuance: even Greyback, a brutal instrument of Voldemort, has his own pride and defiance when his autonomy is challenged. The cellar threat also cements the ongoing sexual predatory dimension of his menace toward Hermione. Both are lost.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film DH2 Scene 13 (Battle of Hogwarts) – Greyback felled quickly by Hermione alone
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Greyback attacks Lavender Brown in a four-legged gray blur and is driven off by Hermione's blast, then finished by a crystal ball dropped by Professor Trelawney. Shortly after, 'Ron and Neville bringing down Fenrir Greyback' is noted as a separate, distinct combat beat. His defeat requires multiple characters and is spread across the battle.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Greyback attacks Lavender, Hermione blasts him with a single deafening shot to the chest and he drops, unmoving. He does not reappear. The Trelawney crystal ball moment and the Ron/Neville defeat beat are absent. Hermione dispatches him entirely alone in a single action.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Minor damage relative to other entries, but the book's version gives the defeat of a major recurring villain more weight and distributes it across multiple characters. The single-shot dismissal by Hermione makes the conclusion of Greyback's arc feel abrupt and low-stakes, though the corpus evidence for the full book battle sequence is sufficient to confirm the divergence.
